title: Kth Largest Element via Quickselect
directAnswer: The kth largest is the (n−k)th smallest, so it sits at 0-indexed position n−k in ascending order. Quickselect partitions around a pivot (Hoare or Lomuto) and recurses into only the side holding index n−k — O(n) average because the work halves each step, O(n²) worst case fixed by a random pivot. The size-k min-heap is the O(n log k) baseline whose top is always the kth largest.

remember.pattern: Quickselect — partition, recurse into one side, target index n − k
remember.formula:
target = n - k                 # 0-indexed position of kth LARGEST (ascending)
lo, hi = 0, n - 1
while lo <= hi:
    p = partition(lo, hi)      # Lomuto: < pivot left, pivot at p
    if p == target: return nums[p]
    elif p < target: lo = p + 1
    else: hi = p - 1
rules: kth **largest** in ascending order = index `n − k`. The mirror of kth smallest (index `k − 1`). Mixing the two formulas is the classic bug.
Quickselect recurses into **one** side only — that's the O(n) average win. Recursing into both is quicksort, O(n log n).
**Lomuto** uses one boundary pointer and is easy to get right; **Hoare** uses two pointers crossing inward — fewer swaps but trickier index returns. Either works; know which you're writing.
Worst case O(n²) hits when the pivot is always extreme (sorted/reverse-sorted input). **Randomize the pivot** (swap a random index into the pivot slot) to make that vanishingly unlikely.
The **size-k min-heap** baseline keeps the k largest seen; its top (the minimum of those k) is the kth largest. O(n log k) time, O(k) space, no worst-case blowup, and it streams.
whenToUse: You need a single order statistic (kth largest, median) from an unsorted, mutable array
Average-case O(n) matters and the input isn't adversarial
In-place is fine — quickselect partitions and reorders the array
For a streaming or memory-bounded variant, fall back to the size-k min-heap
antiSignals: You need the top-k elements sorted, not just the kth → heap or partial sort
Worst-case O(n) is required on adversarial input → median-of-medians, or the heap
Input must stay in original order and can't be copied → quickselect's swaps are out
Repeated kth queries on static data → sort once, index in O(1)
remember.takeaway: Kth largest is kth smallest reflected across the array — target index n − k instead of k − 1. Quickselect reuses the partition primitive and discards half the work each step for O(n) average; the size-k min-heap is the safe O(n log k) fallback. Naming Hoare vs Lomuto and the random-pivot fix is what separates a memorized solution from understanding.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you map kth largest to index n − k cleanly, implement partition correctly (Hoare or Lomuto), and articulate why one-sided recursion is O(n) average while honestly stating the O(n²) worst case.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using the kth-smallest index k − 1 instead of n − k, recursing into both partition halves, or asserting O(n) worst case without a random pivot.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the index mapping out loud, choose Lomuto or Hoare deliberately and say why, add the random-pivot guard unprompted, and offer the size-k min-heap as the streaming-safe alternative with its O(n log k) bound.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **kth largest** element in the array.

Note that it is the kth largest element in sorted order, **not** the kth distinct element — duplicates count toward the rank.

Can you solve it without fully sorting the array?
constraints: Duplicates are allowed and count toward the rank
understanding: Find the element that would occupy 0-indexed position n−k if the array were sorted ascending (equivalently, position k−1 if sorted descending). k = 1 is the maximum. Duplicates are real elements: in [5, 5, 4] the 2nd largest is 5.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is k 1-indexed, and does k = 1 mean the maximum?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — k = 1 is the largest element. In ascending order that's index n − k = n − 1, the last slot.

clarifyingQuestions.question: kth largest counting duplicates, or kth distinct value?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Counting duplicates. In [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], k = 4 returns 4, not the 4th distinct value.

clarifyingQuestions.question: May I reorder the array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Confirm it. Quickselect partitions in place. If the original order must survive, copy first or use the heap.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the input be sorted or adversarial?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If so, a fixed pivot makes quickselect O(n²). Randomize the pivot, or use the size-k min-heap for a hard O(n log k) guarantee.

examples.explanation: Sorted ascending: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. n = 6, target = n − k = 4. Index 4 is 5 — the 2nd largest.
Sorted: [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6]. n = 9, target = 5. Index 5 is 4 — the 4th largest counting duplicates.
Single element; the 1st largest is itself.

approaches.name: Min-Heap of Size k — Baseline
approaches.whenToMention: Offer this first as the clean O(n log k) answer with no worst-case risk — ideal for streams and when you can't mutate the array.
hints: If you keep only the k largest elements seen so far, the smallest among them is the kth largest. What structure exposes the current minimum in O(1) and removes it in O(log k)?
Use a min-heap capped at size k. Push each element; if the heap grows past k, pop the smallest. The heap always holds the k largest seen.
After processing every element, the heap's top (its minimum) is exactly the kth largest of the whole array.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n pushes of O(log k) on a heap bounded by k, plus up to n pops of O(log k) → O(n log k) time. The heap holds at most k elements → O(k) space.
approaches.explanation:
Reframe 'kth largest' as 'the smallest of the k largest'. If you hang onto only the k biggest elements you've seen, then the smallest of those k *is* the kth largest once every element has been processed.

**Why a min-heap, not a max-heap.** You want O(1) access to the *smallest* of your current k keepers, because that's the one most likely to be kicked out when a bigger element arrives. A min-heap puts that smallest on top. Push each new element; if the heap reaches `k + 1`, pop the top (the smallest) — it can't be among the k largest. After the full pass, the heap holds exactly the k largest and its top is the kth largest.

**Why the size cap keeps it fast.** Every heap operation costs `O(log(size))`, and size never exceeds `k`. So although you touch all `n` elements, each costs `O(log k)`. When `k` is small relative to `n`, `O(n log k)` beats the `O(n log n)` of a full sort — and unlike quickselect it never degrades on bad input.

**Why it suits streams.** You only ever hold `k` elements, so data can arrive incrementally and memory stays at `O(k)`. That makes the heap the default when the input is a stream or when space is tight. The cost is the `log k` factor on every element, which quickselect avoids on average at the price of mutating and needing the whole array up front.

**Mirror of kth smallest.** For kth *smallest* you'd use a *max*-heap of size k. The rule of thumb: pick the heap orientation opposite to what you're selecting, so the easiest-to-discard element sits at the top.
approaches.insight: This is the reusable 'keep the best k seen so far' engine — the same one behind Top K Frequent Elements, K Closest Points to Origin, and Kth Largest in a Stream. The only design decision is the comparator: a min-heap to track the largest, a max-heap to track the smallest.

pitfalls: Using a max-heap by reflex — then the top is the largest, not the kth largest.
Forgetting the size cap — the heap grows to n, degrading to O(n log n).
Returning poll() instead of peek() — pop mutates the heap and loses the answer.

approaches.name: Quickselect — Hoare/Lomuto Partition (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer interviewers push toward for O(n) average. Lead with 'kth largest is index n − k; I partition like quicksort but recurse into one side only'.
hints: Quicksort's partition fixes one pivot in its final sorted position p and splits the rest into < pivot and ≥ pivot. If p equals your target index n − k, that pivot is the answer.
If p < target, the answer is in the right part; if p > target, it's in the left. Recurse (or loop) into only that side — never both.
Map kth largest to target = n - k in ascending order. Average work n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n = O(n). Add a random pivot to dodge the O(n²) worst case.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each partition is O(size). An average (roughly balanced) pivot halves the range, so total work telescopes to n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n = O(n). Adversarial input that always selects an extreme pivot gives n + (n−1) + … = O(n²); a random pivot makes that effectively impossible. The iterative loop adds O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Quickselect is quicksort minus the half you don't need. Since you only want one position, you discard the side that can't contain it.

**Index mapping first.** The kth largest in ascending sorted order lives at position `n − k`: the largest (`k = 1`) is at `n − 1`, the smallest-of-the-top-k is further left. Compute `target = n − k` once — this is the entire difference from the kth-*smallest* version, which targets `k − 1`. Getting this mapping right (and not confusing it with `k − 1`) is the first thing to verify aloud.

**The partition primitive — Lomuto.** Pick a pivot (here `nums[hi]`). Sweep `j` from `lo` to `hi−1` with a boundary `i`: each element strictly less than the pivot is swapped to the left of `i`, advancing `i`. Finally swap the pivot into slot `i`. Now `nums[i]` is in its **final sorted position**, smaller elements to its left, ≥ elements to its right. The returned `p = i` is the pivot's true rank.

**Hoare's alternative.** Hoare's scheme runs two pointers inward from both ends, swapping out-of-place pairs until they cross. It performs fewer swaps on average than Lomuto, but its returned split index doesn't land the pivot in its final position, so the recursion boundaries are subtler. Both are valid; Lomuto is easier to reason about under interview pressure, which is why the code below uses it. Mentioning that you *know* Hoare exists and trades fewer swaps for trickier bookkeeping is a strong signal.

**The one-sided shortcut.** Compare `p` to `target`. If `p == target`, return `nums[p]` — done. If `p < target`, the answer is strictly to the right: set `lo = p + 1` and repeat on the right segment only. If `p > target`, set `hi = p − 1`. Recursing into a single side is exactly what turns quicksort's `O(n log n)` into quickselect's `O(n)` average — you throw away half the remaining work each step.

**Average vs worst, and the fix.** A balanced pivot halves the range, telescoping to `2n = O(n)`. But a pivot that is always the max or min — what a fixed last-element pivot does on sorted or reverse-sorted input — shrinks the range by one per step, giving `O(n²)`. The standard guard is a **random pivot**: swap a uniformly random index into the pivot slot before partitioning, so no input ordering can force bad splits. For a hard worst-case guarantee, median-of-medians selects a provably good pivot in `O(n)`, achieving `O(n)` worst case with a larger constant.
approaches.insight: Kth largest and kth smallest are the same algorithm viewed from opposite ends — the only thing that changes is `target = n − k` versus `target = k − 1`. Internalize that reflection and you stop memorizing two solutions. More broadly, quickselect embodies 'compute only the order you were asked for': sorting answers every rank, selection answers one, so selection is cheaper.

pitfalls: Using target = k − 1 (kth smallest) instead of n − k — silently returns the wrong end.
Recursing into both sides — that's quicksort, O(n log n), not quickselect.
Claiming O(n) worst case — it's O(n²) without a random pivot on sorted input.
Hoare partition: returning the wrong boundary index, so the recursion skips or repeats elements.

target = 0 (the minimum); quickselect drives lo/hi to index 0 → returns 1.

commonMistakes: Targeting index k − 1 (kth smallest) instead of n − k for kth largest.
Recursing into both partition sides — collapses quickselect into quicksort.
Using a max-heap instead of a min-heap for the size-k baseline.
Claiming quickselect is O(n) worst case — it's O(n²) without pivot randomization.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong target index
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Kth largest sits at n − k in ascending order. Using k − 1 returns the kth smallest instead — the most common copy-paste bug when adapting the smallest version.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int target = k - 1;        // WRONG: that's the kth SMALLEST
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int target = nums.length - k;   // kth largest in ascending order

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recursing into both sides
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Quickselect's O(n) average comes from discarding the side that can't hold the target. Recursing into both is quicksort — O(n log n).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
p = self._partition(nums, lo, hi)
self.select(nums, lo, p - 1, target)   # WRONG: recurses left
self.select(nums, p + 1, hi, target)   # and right

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Fixed pivot on sorted input
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Always choosing the last element as the pivot makes sorted or reverse-sorted input degrade to O(n²) — each partition peels off a single element.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int pivot = nums[hi];      // fixed pivot → O(n^2) on sorted input

patternNote: Canonical Quickselect (order statistics). Trigger whenever you need a single kth largest/smallest from an unsorted, mutable array and want O(n) average. Reuse quicksort's partition (Hoare or Lomuto) but recurse into one side only; target index n − k for largest, k − 1 for smallest. The size-k heap is the O(n log k) streaming-safe fallback; median-of-medians is the O(n) worst-case variant.
